cards.front: Define a universal family of hash functions H from universe U to slots {0,...,m-1}.
cards.back: H is universal if ∀ distinct x,y ∈ U: |{h ∈ H : h(x)=h(y)}| ≤ |H|/m.

cards.front: What collision probability does universality guarantee when h is chosen uniformly at random from H?
cards.back: Pr[h(x)=h(y)] ≤ 1/m for any fixed distinct x,y.

cards.front: Give the standard linear-universal hash family construction (prime p > |U|).
cards.back: H = {h_{a,b}(x) = ((a·x + b) mod p) mod m | 1≤a≤p-1, 0≤b≤p-1}

cards.front: Derive E[number of colliding pairs] for n keys hashed with universal h into m slots.
cards.back: Let X=∑_{i<j} I_{ij} where I_{ij}=1 if keys i,j collide. Then E[X]=binom(n,2)·(≤1/m) ≤ n²/(2m).

cards.front: Using the pair-collision bound, show expected chain length is O(1+α) in chaining.
cards.back: For a fixed key, E[collisions with it] ≤ (n-1)/m = O(α). Hence total expected lookups = O(1+α).

cards.front: Why does universal hashing give only a probabilistic (not worst-case) guarantee?
cards.back: The O(1+α) bound holds in expectation over random choice of h; a fixed adversarial h may still produce long chains.

cards.front: What is the probability that a specific pair collides under the ax+b family?
cards.back: Exactly 1/m when m divides p-1 or ≤1/m otherwise (standard proof counts solutions for a,b).
